I Was Burning Claude Code Tokens Blind. So I Built a Flight Recorder.

A tiny, free toolkit that tells you where your tokens went, what they would cost, and how to spend fewer

[Your name] · [N] min read

Picture this. You spend an hour with Claude Code, refactoring something gnarly. It goes great. Then you look at your usage and think: "...where did all of that go?"

I had that feeling a few too many times. Claude Code is wonderful, but it is a black box when it comes to tokens. Which skill was the heavy one? Did my coffee break quietly cost me money? Is prompt caching even helping?

So (with Claude's help, naturally) I built a small kit that records every tool call, lets me mark a start and an end, and spits out a report. Here is how it works and how you can use it in about five minutes.

What you get

  • Exact token counts per tool call, read from the session transcript, not guessed.
  • Start and end markers, so you can measure exactly one task.
  • A report with skills used (in order), window time, permission mode, model, effort, and caching details.
  • A cost estimate at API list prices, priced per message with that message's own model.
  • Skills flow and tool flow diagrams, so you can literally see what happened.
  • Optimization tips, but only the ones your own data justifies.

Everything is local. No network calls, no dependencies beyond Python's standard library.

How it works (the 30-second version)

Claude Code supports hooks: small scripts that run at certain moments. Mine runs after every tool call, peeks at the session transcript (where the real token counts already live), and appends one line to a log file. Slash commands drop markers into that same log, and a reader script turns the log into reports.

That is it. No magic, no proxy sitting between you and the API.

Install in one command

The kit ships as a single file, install_token_log.py, with everything embedded and verified by a checksum. Nothing to unzip:

python3 install_token_log.py              # install or update
python3 install_token_log.py --dry-run    # preview, change nothing
python3 install_token_log.py --check      # see what is installed
python3 install_token_log.py --uninstall  # remove it (keeps your log)

A few things I cared about when writing the installer:

  • It backs up your settings.json before touching it, and merges instead of overwriting.
  • It runs a self-test (hook, reader, report) before registering anything. If the test fails, it installs the files but leaves your hooks alone and tells you why.
  • Re-running it is safe.

Restart Claude Code afterwards and you are set.

Heads up: I tested everything on macOS/Linux-style setups with synthetic data. Windows support is untested. If something breaks there, --python and --no-settings are your escape hatches.

The three-command ritual

This is the part you will actually use:

/token-start refactor      # drop a marker
... do your normal work ...
/token-end refactor        # tokens consumed between the marks
/token-report refactor     # the full report

Give the window a name if you like, or skip it and it uses "default". Need a peek mid-task without closing the window? /token-span shows the running total.

Reading the report

The report is plain markdown, saved to ~/.claude/token-reports/. Here is the map of what is inside:

The sections I look at first:

  • Window: total time, split into active and idle. Idle time is a quiet hint that your cache may have expired.
  • Tokens: new tokens versus cache reads. Cache reads are the cheap ones; new input and output are where the money goes.
  • Estimated cost: broken down by output, input, cache writes and cache reads.
  • Caching: hit rate and how much the cache saved you.

Seeing the flow

My favorite part. The report draws two flows: the order your skills ran in, and the order of every tool call, with time and context growth on each step.

In the report file itself these are Mermaid diagrams, which GitHub and VS Code's Markdown preview render automatically. Everywhere else you will see the diagram source plus a plain table with the same facts.

The cache plot twist

This one surprised me. Prompt caching makes re-reading your context cheap, but the default cache only lives for a few minutes. Step away for a long coffee, come back, and your next message may pay to write the entire context into the cache again.

The report checks for exactly this. If it sees a long pause followed by a big cache write, it flags it and shows the evidence. Whether a longer cache lifetime is available depends on your setup, so check the current docs for your plan before relying on it.

About the cost number

Quick honesty section, because cost numbers are easy to misread:

  • Prices come from a pricing.json file based on the official pricing page (retrieved 2026-10-31). Prices change, so edit the file when they do.
  • If you are on a Pro, Max or Team subscription, you are not billed per token. Read the figure as "what this would cost at API prices".
  • It leaves out fast mode, data residency and batch multipliers, and server-side web tool fees.
  • A model that is not in the table shows up as "Not priced" instead of a made-up number.

The tips (and why I trust them a bit)

The suggestions are rule-based, not vibes. Each tip shows the evidence it measured and what to do about it. The rules cover things like:

  • Cache expiry during pauses
  • Switching models in the middle of a task
  • Context compaction
  • Heavy skills that add a lot of context
  • Huge tool outputs
  • A big model doing routine work

They are heuristics from one window, not guarantees. Treat them as "worth a look", not gospel.

My honest limits list

  • It was tested on synthetic data and simulated sessions. Please try it on a real session and tell me what breaks.
  • Effort level and permission mode come from the hook payload, and a couple of environment variable names for caching come from unofficial sources. Verify them on your version.
  • Settings that live only in settings.json are not visible to the hook.
  • Durations run until the next step starts, so they include your own thinking and pauses.

Try it

Install it, run one /token-start and /token-report around your next task, and look at the cache section first. I would be surprised if it does not teach you something about your own habits.
